notes.purpose: A record of what the video engine does with what inputs. Every entry is a file a desktop player opens without complaint; whether a browser decodes it is the question the matrix answers rather than assumes.
notes.inclusionRule: If VLC or QuickTime would not play it, it is not in the matrix. A zero-byte file or a JPEG renamed .mp4 proves nothing, because nothing plays those. The product risk is the file that works everywhere else and not here.
notes.notACrossProduct: The axes below multiply out to millions of combinations, and encoding them would take weeks and answer nothing new: a codec bug does not hide behind a timebase. The matrix is a spine of one-axis-at-a-time variations off a single baseline, plus a handful of combinations named as such, which is where interactions actually live.
notes.derivedQuantitiesNotKnobs: The load axes are derived quantities, not encoder knobs. A frame-rate sweep moves pixel throughput, frame budget and frames-per-GOP together and cannot say which one bit; 15 fps at 8 MP and 120 fps at 1 MP demand almost the same throughput and give an eight-fold different budget to meet it in, and that pair says something a sweep cannot. Codec, container, timebase and rotation stay as themselves, because they are correctness axes rather than load ones.
notes.heldConstant: Every encoded clip is a short excerpt of one of the two real sources, re-encoded at a small size, so content is held constant and only the encoding varies. Changing the declared frame rate changes how fast the content plays; that is expected and does not affect frame identity, because ordinals map one to one through the pipeline.
notes.stamping: Every encoded clip carries its frame index in its own pixels. The 16-bit stamp addresses 65,536 frames; a clip longer than that sets stampWraps and its identity checks are modulo 65,536. The two reference entries are unmodified originals and carry no stamp.
notes.reproducibility: Every clip is byte-reproducible on a fixed ffmpeg build and thread count except the bytes-per-GOP sweep, whose x264 rate control does not settle to the same output twice. Those declare reproducible: false and their digests record what a run produced rather than what a rebuild will match.
notes.declaredRateAxis: The 10x mismatch large.mp4 carries (600 declared, 56.4 delivered) does not reproduce synthetically: ffprobe derives r_frame_rate from the whole duration table, not from the shortest interval, so a hand-built pattern lands nearer 2x. reference-large-screen carries the extreme end of this axis; declared-rate-lie and declared-rate-honest bracket it.
notes.identityOracle: The stamp read off a presented frame is compared against that frame presentation ordinal, which is what PresentedFrameId.index carries and what frame-timeline.ts binary-searches the container tick table for. No frame rate appears in the comparison. The engine also publishes MediaFrameDiagnostics.estimatedFrameIndex, which is round((t - t0) x rate) seeded from a 120-packet prefix; the matrix records that per clip as engineFrameRateReading and never asserts against it, because on large.mp4 the prefix reads 57.07 fps against a true 56.38 and the published index is 2,856 frames wrong by the end.
notes.stampAffectsBytes: Every clip except baseline-unstamped and the two references carries a drawn stamp, which adds bytes on a CRF encode and steals them on the CBR bytes-per-GOP arms. Read any byte figure against baseline-unstamped rather than as the file own.
notes.referenceEntries: The two originals are probed in place and recorded by digest. They are never copied into the repository and never re-encoded.

sources.why: 2840x2840 at 15 fps in Constrained Baseline: 8.07 MP a frame and about 10.3 MB a GOP, so every seek fetches ten megabytes before it can decode anything.
69 minutes and 233,059 frames, declaring 600 fps while delivering 56.4: 23% of the million-frame ceiling and a frame rate that lies by a factor of ten.

axes.pixelThroughput: fps x megapixels: what the decoder and the texture upload must sustain, and 1/fps, the time there is to do it in
axes.gopBytes: what a seek has to fetch before it can decode anything; the metric, not GOP seconds
axes.framesPerGop: how many frames a seek walks from the keyframe before it reaches the target
axes.keyframeBytes: the minimum fetch before anything can be shown
axes.frameCount: what opening pays, because building the frame table walks every packet; and distance toward the million-frame ceiling
axes.declaredFrameRate: what the container claims against what it delivers
axes.profileEfficiency: what the codec profile alone costs in bytes, and so in seek time
axes.shape: square, portrait, and dimensions aligned to no macroblock
axes.codec: what the browser has to have a decoder for
axes.container: how the bytes are wrapped, and when the index arrives
axes.gopStructure: all-intra, open GOP, and everything between
axes.bFrames: how far decode order diverges from presentation order
axes.frameRate: the fractional rates and the variable timing where index arithmetic drifts; deliberately not a load sweep
axes.exactCacheMode: which of the exact frame cache two limits binds, a byte budget or a 13-slot floor, which swap places at 2.5811 MP a frame. Both real files sit on the floor at 13 slots, and a clip below the flip is measured with a cache several times deeper than they get.
axes.stampCost: what drawing the frame stamp adds to a clip bytes, so every other byte figure can be read against a control
axes.timebase: the tick table decoded timestamps get snapped onto
axes.startTimestamp: whether media time and elapsed time are the same number
axes.rotation: the display matrix every phone writes
axes.chroma: 4:2:2, 4:4:4 and higher bit depths an editor emits
axes.legacyCodec: what a desktop player opens and a browser has never had a decoder for
axes.extension: right content, wrong name; people rename files
axes.combination: the interactions a one-axis spine cannot reach
